```{r setup}
library(moleculaR)
```

## About the package

`moleculaR` replicates the central dogma of molecular biology: DNA is transcribed into mRNA, and mRNA is translated into protein. It has one function for each step, from generating a random DNA sequence to plotting the amino acid composition of the resulting protein. It also includes `codon_table`, a standard codon table that maps each of the 64 RNA codons to the one-letter code of the amino acid it encodes (stop codons are written as `"_"`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Install from GitHub
devtools::install_github("rforbiodatascience26/group_8_package")
```

## The functions

This package will replicate the central dogma of molecular biology.

### 1. Generate DNA sequence

**`generate_DNAseq()`** creates a random DNA sequence of a given length by sampling the bases A, T, G and C.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
generate_DNAseq(12)
```

### 2. Transcribe all T bases to U

**`transcribe()`** turns DNA into mRNA by replacing every T with U.

```{r}
transcribe("ATGCATTGA")
```

### 3. Extract codons

**`extract_codons()`** splits a sequence into codons (triplets). `start` sets the reading frame; leftover bases that don't form a full codon are dropped.

```{r}
extract_codons("AUGCAUUGA")
extract_codons("AUGCAUUGA", start = 2)
```

### 4. Get Codon

**`get_codon()`** translates codons into a protein sequence by looking each one up in `codon_table` and joining the amino acids into one string.

```{r}
get_codon(c("AUG", "CAU", "UGA"))
```

### 5. Plot Amino Acid Counts

**`plot_aa_counts()`** counts how often each amino acid (character) occurs in a sequence and shows the counts as a bar chart. It uses `ggplot2` and `stringr`.

## Using the functions together

The output of each function is the input to the next, so the whole central dogma can be run as one pipeline:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 2.6, fig.align = "center"}
set.seed(42)
protein <- generate_DNAseq(150) |>
  transcribe() |>
  extract_codons() |>
  get_codon()
protein
plot_aa_counts(protein)
```



## Use cases and possible extensions

`moleculaR` is useful for teaching and illustrating the central dogma, for generating random test sequences, and for a quick overview of the amino acid composition of a short sequence. Random sequences can also serve as a simple null model, e.g. to see how often stop codons appear by chance.

The package has clear limitations: translation does not look for a start codon (AUG) and continues past stop codons, and random DNA has an even base composition, unlike real genomes. Functions that could be added include a reverse complement, GC content, finding open reading frames, translating all six reading frames, reading sequences from FASTA files, and simulating mutations.

## Group discussion

- **Adding dependencies:** `plot_aa_counts()` needs `ggplot2` and `stringr`. We added them with `usethis::use_package("ggplot2")` and `usethis::use_package("stringr")`, which lists them under `Imports` in the `DESCRIPTION` file so they are installed together with `moleculaR`.
- **Why limit dependencies:** every dependency has to be installed by users, can change or break between versions, and makes the package harder to maintain. They can't always be avoided: writing our own plotting or string handling would be more work and more error-prone than relying on well-tested packages.
- **`@importFrom` vs. `package::function()`:** `@importFrom` adds the function to the package's `NAMESPACE`, so it can be called without a prefix. `package::function()` shows explicitly in the code where a function comes from, which makes the code easier to read. Either way, the package must be listed in `DESCRIPTION`.
